final_answer:
Short answer: the office that can lawfully bring ALL of the doctor's false claims (both states) in one indictment, and failing that the office that holds the larger share of the loss/counts and moves first, should indict. No single office is fixed by law; the Guidelines drive the answer.

1. Venue limits the choice. Venue lies where the offense was committed; for offenses begun, continued or completed in more than one district, 18 U.S.C. 3237(a) allows prosecution in any district in which the offense was begun, continued or completed. If the Georgia and South Carolina claims are one scheme to defraud executed in both states, either district may have venue over the whole scheme. If they are separate schemes (each execution of a scheme is a separate 1347 offense), each district has venue only over the claims made there, and neither office can indict the other state's conduct as a charged offense. (I could not retrieve the text of 3237 or 1347 directly; description comes from search summaries.)

2. Why one consolidated prosecution gives the most time. Section 1347 carries up to 10 years per count (20 if serious bodily injury, life if death). Under the Guidelines, multiple fraud counts are grouped and the loss is aggregated (USSG 3D1.2(d), 2B1.1), so a single sentencing court sees the total loss from both states and sets one combined offense level; where the guideline range exceeds the statutory maximum of the highest count, USSG 5G1.2(d) lets the court run counts consecutively to reach the total punishment. Even in a single-state prosecution, uncharged other-state fraud can be relevant conduct under USSG 1B1.3(a)(2) (same course of conduct or common scheme) and so raises that court's loss figure. (These Guidelines points are from my knowledge; I could not fetch the Commission text.)

3. Why two sequential prosecutions are worse for prosecutors. If the first district sentences the doctor and the second prosecution is for conduct that was relevant conduct in the first, USSG 5G1.3(b) requires the second sentence to run concurrently with the undischarged term (with adjustment for time served), so the second case adds little or no time; only if the conduct is not relevant conduct does 5G1.3(d) leave consecutive sentencing discretionary. Also the double-counting overlap means the second office gains little. The practical rule: the office with venue over the entire scheme and the greater loss should indict first (or the two offices should agree on one district, with the other deferring or the case transferred under Fed. R. Crim. P. 21/22 consent), because the aggregated loss and consecutive-stacking authority sit with one sentencing judge.

4. Application. Absent facts, choose whichever district has venue over the whole scheme; if each has venue only for its own state, the office with the larger loss/more counts should indict first, since its aggregated guideline range (including the other state's relevant conduct) and statutory-maximum stacking yield the longest sentence, and the other office's later case would largely run concurrently under 5G1.3(b). Caveats: Guidelines are advisory (Booker), judges may vary; double jeopardy does not bar separate-sovereign-free but same-sovereign successive prosecutions only if same offense (Blockburger), which separate schemes are not; DOJ policy (Petite-type/coordination) favors one forum.
